solution:
**Propan-1-ol** (n-propyl alcohol), \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-OH}\).

In hydroboration - oxidation the alkene first adds diborane \(\mathrm{(B_2H_6)}\) to give a trialkylborane, which is then oxidised by hydrogen peroxide in alkaline medium. The overall result is **antimarkownikoff hydration** of the alkene, so the \(\mathrm{-OH}\) goes to the terminal (less substituted) carbon of propene and the product is the primary alcohol.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH{=}CH_2} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(ii)}\ \mathrm{H_2O_2},\ \mathrm{{}^{\ominus}OH}]{\mathrm{(i)}\ \mathrm{B_2H_6}\text{ - THF}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-OH}\)

**2-Methylpropan-2-ol**, \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-OH}\) (tert-butyl alcohol).

Of the four alcohols of molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}O}\) — butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol — only 2-methylpropan-2-ol is **tertiary**: its carbinol carbon carries three methyl groups and no hydrogen. Oxidation of an alcohol to a carbonyl compound needs a hydrogen on that carbon, so this alcohol is the one resistant towards oxidation. The chapter states that tertiary alcohols are difficult to oxidise and react only with strong oxidising agents at high temperature, and then by breaking \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bonds.

**Butan-2-ol**, \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_2-CH_3}\) (sec-butyl alcohol).

The four alcohols of molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}O}\) are butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol. In butan-2-ol the carbon carrying \(\mathrm{-OH}\) is bonded to four **different** groups — \(\mathrm{-OH}\), \(\mathrm{-H}\), \(\mathrm{-CH_3}\) and \(\mathrm{-C_2H_5}\) — so it is the only one of the four that can exist as a pair of non-superimposable mirror images and hence be optically active. Each of the other three has at least two identical groups on the carbinol carbon.

[Note: this chapter itself does not develop optical activity; the reasoning above rests on the general condition for it, and the chapter supplies only the four isomeric structures.]

**Carbon dioxide**, \(\mathrm{CO_2}\).

In Kolbe's reaction sodium phenoxide is treated with carbon dioxide at 398 K under a pressure of 6 atm, followed by acid hydrolysis, to give salicylic acid (o-hydroxybenzoic acid). The chapter notes that sodium phenoxide is more reactive than phenol towards electrophilic substitution, which is why it is able to react with a **weak electrophile like** \(\mathrm{CO_2}\).

The acid strength of a compound depends on how well its **conjugate base** is stabilised.

On losing \(\mathrm{H^{\oplus}}\), phenol gives the **phenoxide ion**, whose negative charge is delocalised over the benzene ring through five resonance structures. This resonance stabilisation makes the phenoxide ion a relatively stable anion, so phenol ionises in aqueous medium to a moderate extent and shows weak acidic character.

Ethyl alcohol on losing \(\mathrm{H^{\oplus}}\) gives the **ethoxide ion**, \(\mathrm{CH_3 \rightarrow CH_2 \rightarrow O^{\ominus}}\), in which the negative charge stays localised on the oxygen. Worse, the electron-donating inductive effect \((+\mathrm{I})\) of the alkyl group pushes electron density towards that oxygen and **destabilises** the alkoxide. As a result ethyl alcohol does not ionise much in water and behaves like a neutral compound.

Because the phenoxide ion is stabilised while the ethoxide ion is destabilised, phenol is more acidic than ethyl alcohol. This is also seen in the laboratory: aqueous phenol turns blue litmus red while aqueous ethyl alcohol is neutral to litmus.

Again the comparison is between the two conjugate bases.

The conjugate base of phenol, the phenoxide ion, is resonance stabilised by **five** resonance structures.

In p-nitrophenol the \(\mathrm{-NO_2}\) group at the para position is strongly electron-withdrawing, and the negative charge of the phenoxide can be delocalised onto the oxygens of the nitro group as well. Its conjugate base is therefore better resonance stabilised, having **six** resonance structures. Of these, the sixth carries the negative charge on **only electronegative oxygen atoms**, which is a particularly favourable arrangement.

The better stabilised the conjugate base, the stronger the acid. Hence p-nitrophenol is a stronger acid than phenol.

Two points of difference, both drawn from the chapter's laboratory tests :

**1. Action on litmus.** An aqueous solution of phenol turns blue litmus **red**, showing that phenol has acidic character. An aqueous solution of ethyl alcohol is **neutral** to litmus — it changes neither blue nor red litmus.

**2. Reaction with aqueous NaOH.** Phenol dissolves in aqueous \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) forming water-soluble sodium phenoxide, and is regenerated on acidification with HCl :

\(\mathrm{Ar-OH} + \mathrm{NaOH(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ar-O^{\ominus}Na^{\oplus}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2O}(l)\)

Ethyl alcohol shows no acidic character in aqueous solution and does **not** react with aqueous \(\mathrm{NaOH}\).

(A third difference, if wanted : phenol reacts with neutral ferric chloride solution to give a deep purple/violet/green colouration of ferric phenoxide, whereas ethyl alcohol gives no such colour.)

**a. From chlorobenzene (Dow process).** Reagent : aqueous/fused \(\mathrm{NaOH}\). Conditions : high temperature and pressure, **623 K and 300 atm**; the sodium phenoxide so formed is then treated with **dilute HCl**.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-Cl} \xrightarrow[623\ \mathrm{K}\ /\ 300\ \mathrm{atm}]{\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-O^{\ominus}Na^{\oplus}} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^{\oplus}}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-OH}\)

**b. From benzene sulfonic acid.** Reagents : \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) for neutralisation, then **solid** \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) for fusion, then dilute acid. Conditions : the fusion with solid \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) is carried out at **573 K**.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-SO_3H} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-SO_3Na} \xrightarrow[573\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-O^{\ominus}Na^{\oplus}} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. HCl}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-OH}\)

Isopropyl benzene is **cumene**, and this is the commercial method of preparing phenol. Cumene on air oxidation in presence of Co-naphthenate gives cumene hydroperoxide, which on decomposition with dilute acid gives phenol, with acetone as a valuable by-product.

**Step 1 — air oxidation :**

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH(CH_3)_2} + \mathrm{O_2} \xrightarrow[423\ \mathrm{K}]{\text{Co-naphthenate}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-C(CH_3)_2-O-O-H}\)

(Cumene) + (air) \(\longrightarrow\) (Cumene hydroperoxide)

**Step 2 — acid decomposition :**

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-C(CH_3)_2-O-O-H} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{dil. HCl}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-OH} + \mathrm{CH_3-CO-CH_3}\)

(Cumene hydroperoxide) \(\longrightarrow\) (Phenol) + (Acetone)

**Test with sodium metal.**

Ethanol contains an alcoholic \(\mathrm{-OH}\) group. When a small piece of sodium metal is added to it, brisk effervescence occurs and **hydrogen gas is liberated**, leaving sodium ethoxide in solution :

\(2\,\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-OH} + 2\mathrm{Na} \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-O^{\ominus}Na^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{H_2}\uparrow\)

Ethyl bromide, \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-Br}\), has no \(\mathrm{-OH}\) group, so no hydrogen is evolved.

The chapter states that liberation of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) gas on treatment with an active metal is used to detect the presence of an alcoholic \(\mathrm{-OH}\) group in a molecule, so the compound that gives the gas is ethanol and the one that does not is ethyl bromide.

[Textbook misprint: the book prints "oxidation of (B) gave and acid (D)" and "compound (B)and (C)". The first is a slip for "gave an acid (D)" and is preserved exactly as printed; the sense is not in doubt, since (D) is contrasted with the ketone (E) in the same sentence. Separately, the data given do not determine the ether uniquely — the model answer below names the alternative that also fits.]

**Reading the clues.** Oxidation of (B) gives a carboxylic **acid**, so (B) is a **primary** alcohol. Oxidation of (C) gives a **ketone**, so (C) is a **secondary** alcohol. (B) and (C) come from hydrolysis of the two alkyl iodides, so the ether (A) must be built from one primary and one secondary alkyl group totalling five carbons.

**(A) = ethyl isopropyl ether**, \(\mathrm{C_2H_5-O-CH(CH_3)_2}\), which is \(\mathrm{C_5H_{12}O}\).

With hot HI the ether is first cleaved, and the chapter notes that with **excess** HI the alcohol formed in the first stage is itself converted into the alkyl iodide — so both fragments end up as alkyl halides :

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5-O-CH(CH_3)_2} \xrightarrow{\text{excess hot HI}} \mathrm{C_2H_5-I} + \mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH-I}\)

Hydrolysis of the two iodides gives

**(B)** \(= \mathrm{C_2H_5-OH}\) (ethanol, a primary alcohol)

**(C)** \(= \mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH-OH}\) (propan-2-ol, a secondary alcohol)

Oxidation then gives

**(D)** \(= \mathrm{CH_3-COOH}\) (acetic acid) — a primary alcohol oxidises through the aldehyde to a carboxylic acid with the same number of carbon atoms;

**(E)** \(= \mathrm{CH_3-CO-CH_3}\) (propan-2-one, acetone) — a secondary alcohol oxidises to a ketone.

[Note: the data as printed do not single this out uniquely — methyl sec-butyl ether, \(\mathrm{CH_3-O-CH(CH_3)-C_2H_5}\), is also \(\mathrm{C_5H_{12}O}\) and would give methanol and butan-2-ol, hence formic acid and butan-2-one, satisfying every stated condition as well. Ethyl isopropyl ether is given here because it is the compound this chapter itself works with.]

**3-Methoxyhexane** — the parent alkane is hexane (six carbons in a chain) and a methoxy group \(\mathrm{(-O-CH_3)}\) is attached at C-3 :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH(O-CH_3)-CH_2-CH_2-CH_3}\)

**Methyl vinyl ether** — a common-system name, so the two groups attached to the ethereal oxygen are simply named: a methyl group \(\mathrm{(-CH_3)}\) and a vinyl group \(\mathrm{(-CH{=}CH_2)}\) :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-O-CH{=}CH_2}\)

**1-Ethylcyclohexanol** — a cyclic alcohol, so the parent is cyclohexane with the \(\mathrm{-OH}\) group taken as attached to the C-1 carbon atom; an ethyl group \(\mathrm{(-C_2H_5)}\) is attached at that same C-1.

Structure : a six-membered carbon ring in which one ring carbon carries both \(\mathrm{-OH}\) and \(\mathrm{-C_2H_5}\), the remaining five ring carbons each carrying two hydrogens.

Condensed formula : \(\mathrm{C_6H_{10}(C_2H_5)(OH)}\), i.e. \(\mathrm{C_8H_{16}O}\).

**Pentane-1,4-diol** — the parent is pentane; the ending 'e' is retained, 'diol' shows two \(\mathrm{-OH}\) groups, and the locants 1 and 4 give their positions :

\(\mathrm{HO-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-CH(OH)-CH_3}\)

**Cyclohex-2-en-1-ol** — a cyclic alcohol built on cyclohexene. The \(\mathrm{-OH}\) is at C-1 and the carbon-carbon double bond lies between C-2 and C-3.

Structure : a six-membered carbon ring carrying \(\mathrm{-OH}\) on C-1, a \(\mathrm{C{=}C}\) double bond between C-2 and C-3, and \(\mathrm{-CH_2-}\) groups at C-4, C-5 and C-6.

Molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_6H_{10}O}\). Note that the \(\mathrm{-OH}\)-bearing C-1 is \(\mathrm{sp^3}\) and is bonded to an \(\mathrm{sp^2}\) carbon of the double bond, so this is an **allylic** alcohol.

**1-Methylcyclopentan-1-ol.**

The ring is a five-membered carbon ring, so the parent is cyclopentane. It is a cyclic alcohol, so the \(\mathrm{-OH}\)-bearing carbon is numbered C-1 and the ending 'e' of cyclopentane is replaced by 'ol'. The same C-1 also carries a methyl group, which is named as the substituent prefix with locant 1.

**2-Methylbutane-1,3-diol.**

The longest chain carrying both \(\mathrm{-OH}\) groups has four carbons, so the parent is butane. Numbering from the \(\mathrm{-CH_2-OH}\) end puts the two hydroxyl groups at C-1 and C-3, i.e. locants \(\{1,3\}\); numbering from the other end would put them at C-2 and C-4, i.e. \(\{2,4\}\), which is higher. So numbering starts at the \(\mathrm{-CH_2-OH}\) end.

With two \(\mathrm{-OH}\) groups the 'e' of butane is retained and 'diol' is added, and the methyl branch sits on C-2.

**2-Nitrophenol** (o-nitrophenol).

The compound is a hydroxyl derivative of benzene, i.e. a phenol, and the common name phenol is accepted by IUPAC. The \(\mathrm{-NO_2}\) group is on the ring carbon **adjacent** to the one carrying \(\mathrm{-OH}\). The \(\mathrm{-OH}\)-bearing carbon is C-1, so the nitro group takes the locant 2. The chapter's common-name equivalent for this position is the prefix **ortho**, so it is also written o-nitrophenol.

**Methoxycyclohexane.**

The compound is an ether: an oxygen joins a cyclohexane ring to a methyl group. Under the IUPAC system ethers are named as **alkoxyalkanes**, the larger alkyl group being taken as the parent. Here the larger group is the six-membered ring, so the parent is cyclohexane, and the smaller group appears as the prefix methoxy \(\mathrm{(CH_3-O-)}\). No locant is needed because every position on the unsubstituted ring is equivalent.

(In the common system, in which the two groups attached to oxygen are named in alphabetical order followed by the word ether, the same compound is cyclohexyl methyl ether.)
